title: How Do I Identify Rice Pests From a Photo?
metaTitle: Identify Rice Pests From a Photo: What to Shoot and Check
metaDescription: Learn to identify rice pests from a photo: which pictures to take, the damage each pest leaves, the look alikes, and when a count means you should act.
focusKeyword: identify rice pests from a photo
keywords: identify rice pests from a photo
excerpt: To identify rice pests from a photo, take two pictures: a close one of the insect and one of the damage it left, both sharp and in daylight. Then match the damage to the pest: deadhearts and whiteheads point to stem borers, yellow and dried patches with insects at the base point to planthoppers, and empty grains point to rice bugs. With anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, you can send the photo to Anee, its smart farm technician, or match the damage in the free Pest Finder.

blocks.text:
Often, a photo of the damage helps more than a photo of the insect. Many rice pests hide at the base of the plant or fly off before you get close, but the damage stays. Also, many insects in a paddy are not pests at all. Spiders, dragonflies and many small wasps eat the pests, and a photo full of them is good news.

IRRI also notes that different causes can leave the same mark. Deadhearts and whiteheads, for example, can come from stem borers, rats, neck blast or black bugs. So a good photo set shows three things: the insect, the damage and the pattern in the field.

items: Take three photos: the insect up close, the damage, and the hill or patch around it.
Shoot in the early morning or late afternoon, the hours PalayCheck gives for monitoring insect pests.
Match the damage, not just the bug, with the table below.
Confirm with a field check, like pulling a tiller or tapping the base of the hill, before you spray.
In anee.io, send the photo to Anee or match the damage in the free Pest Finder.

items.title: Go early or late
items.text: Walk the field from 5 to 7 in the morning or late in the afternoon. PalayCheck gives these hours for monitoring insect pests, since many move or hide later in the day.

items.title: Shoot the insect
items.text: Fill the frame with it, in sharp focus, from the side and from above. Put a coin or your finger beside it to show its size.

items.title: Shoot the damage
items.text: Take the leaf, the stem base or the panicle where the harm is. For a dead center tiller, pull it and photograph its base too.

items.title: Shoot the pattern
items.text: Step back and take the hill, then the patch or the whole field. Patches, rows and field edges each tell a different story.

items.title: Tap the base
items.text: Grasp a hill, bend it over a little and tap it near the base, as IRRI advises for planthoppers. Then photograph what falls on the water.

items.title: Write it down
items.text: Note the lot, the variety and the days after transplanting, because many pests strike at certain stages.

blocks.text: Which rice pest left this damage?
Match what your photo shows with the first column. Then do the check in the last column before you decide anything.

blocks.text: Look alikes that fool a photo

Hopperburn and the bugburn of black bugs look alike from the bund. IRRI's check is simple: planthoppers leave honeydew and sooty mold at the base, while black bug damage has none. Also, you cannot pull out a plant hit by black bugs, but a stem borer deadheart comes out easily.

Rice bug damage can look like a nutrient problem or flower thrips, so look for the bugs themselves. Not sure it is an insect at all? Read [how to tell a pest from a disease](/blog/pest-or-disease-how-to-tell), and see our guide to the [golden apple snail](/pests/golden-apple-snail) for snail damage.
When does a photo mean you should act?

One insect in a photo is not a reason to spray. IRRI says that at 1 brown planthopper per stem or fewer, there is still time to act if the numbers rise. For rice bugs, IRRI says you may need direct control above 10 bugs per 20 hills. PalayCheck also sets levels for each growth stage, so count before you decide. Our guide to [early pest detection](/blog/early-pest-detection) has the full table.

blocks.title: Spraying early can make it worse
blocks.text: IRRI notes that planthopper outbreaks follow pesticides that destroy their natural enemies. If you do spray, use a product registered with the FPA for rice and for that pest, and follow the label.

items.q: Can I identify a rice pest from a blurry photo?
items.a: Rarely. Retake it in daylight with the insect or the damage filling the frame. A second photo of the whole hill helps too.

items.q: What if I only see damage and no insect?
items.a: That is common, since many pests hide or fly off. Match the damage in the table above or in the Pest Finder. Then go back in the early morning and look for the insect at the base of the hills.

items.q: Are all insects in the paddy pests?
items.a: No. Spiders, dragonflies, damselflies and many small wasps feed on rice pests. A field with plenty of them may not need any spray at all.

items.q: Can Anee identify rice pests from a photo in Tagalog?
items.a: Yes. Ask in Tagalog, Bisaya, Ilocano, Taglish or English and add the photo. This needs a plan with Anee, and each answer uses credits.

items.q: When should I call the municipal agriculturist?
items.a: Call when the damage spreads fast, covers patches, or your count passes the action level. The office can confirm the pest and advise on control for your area.
